A product manager preparing a roadmap decision.

Decision memo / Draft

Should we prioritize onboarding?

We should prioritize onboarding next quarter because new users are dropping off. A shorter setup will improve activation and reduce churn, making it our highest-impact opportunity.

Original draft · Your words stay yours

Bring your own evidence into this workflow preview. Your note stays in your browser.

Writing partners

Assumption · Still unresolved

Drop-off does not explain its cause.

The draft jumps from “users stop” to “setup is too long,” then from activation to churn. Both links need evidence.

A question worth answering

What would distinguish setup friction from low intent or missing product value?

Trace the argument
  • Claim: onboarding is the best opportunity.
  • Evidence: a drop-off sample, supplied by the author.
  • Assumption: setup length causes drop-off.
  • Tradeoff: onboarding work displaces other roadmap bets.
  • Counterargument: the real problem may be weak intent or value.

Suggested edit · You decide

Make the uncertainty readable.

Your evidence note

Add your evidence in the Reasoning tab before approving this edit.

Why this edit?

Separate the observation from the hypothesis. Replace a guaranteed outcome with a test. Keep the original intent visible.

Workflow preview · Fluency is not proof.

For the person accountable for the decision

A better memo starts with a better argument.

For product managers writing consequential proposals in Notion: onboarding bets, roadmap tradeoffs, and experiment plans. The goal is a memo your team can interrogate, not a paragraph that merely sounds confident.

“the writer is the first reader”

Paul Graham, Good Writing (May 2025)

Graham connects clear prose with well-developed ideas. Revision can uncover weak reasoning; easier rereading makes gaps easier to notice. But an elegant argument can still start from a false premise.

Diya Lamp brings a structured review with evidence, questions, and individually approved edits. Not another general-purpose chat box. It helps you inspect a decision; it does not certify truth.

The words and the reasoning move together.

01 / Draft

Make the bet explicit.

“Shorter setup will reduce churn.”

An attractive sentence with two untested links.

02 / Challenge

Ask what supports it.

Does setup friction cause drop-off? Does activation affect retention?

Reasoning agent flags the gaps.

03 / Respond

Add evidence, not confidence.

18 of 40 stopped during setup. Cause and retention impact remain unknown.

The author supplies context.

04 / Revise

Turn certainty into a test.

Test whether a shorter setup improves activation before committing the quarter.

Clarity agent suggests; author approves.

Step 1 of 4: begin with the draft.

Built around author ownership.
